lesson.title: One Character at a Time: Working with Individual Letters
lesson.summary: Because Python has no separate character type, indexing a string gives back a length-1 string, so every string method, including validation methods, works on a single character exactly as it does on a whole word.
lesson.body:
Python does not have a separate character data type the way some languages do. When you index into a string with something like word[0], the result is not a special 'char' value, it is simply another string, just one that happens to have a length of 1. This is a subtle but important idea, because it means every string method you already know, including the validation methods like isalpha() and isdigit(), works exactly the same way on a single character as it does on a full word, since as far as Python is concerned there is no difference in kind, only in length.

This lets you reason about text one symbol at a time. Suppose word = "Python7". Indexing word[0] gives 'P', a string of length 1, and you can immediately ask word[0].isupper(), which returns True. Indexing word[6] gives '7', and word[6].isdigit() returns True while word[6].isalpha() returns False. Because each character is just a tiny string, you can chain the same dot-notation calls you use on whole strings, which means there is nothing new to memorize here beyond the fact that indexing produces a length-1 string rather than some other type.

Two built-in functions round out character-level work, even though they are functions rather than methods: ord() and chr(). ord() takes a single character and returns its underlying numeric code point, so ord('A') is 65 and ord('a') is 97. chr() does the reverse, taking a number and returning the one-character string at that code point, so chr(65) is 'A'. These are useful for tasks like shifting letters in a simple cipher, or checking whether one letter comes before another in the alphabet by comparing their numeric codes directly instead of trusting intuition.

A common use of character-level reasoning is scanning a string with a loop and testing each character in turn. Consider counting the vowels in a word: vowels = "aeiou", count = 0, then for letter in "banana": if letter in vowels: count += 1. Tracing this by hand, the loop visits 'b', 'a', 'n', 'a', 'n', 'a' in order. 'b' is not in "aeiou" so count stays 0. 'a' is in "aeiou" so count becomes 1. 'n' is skipped. The next 'a' brings count to 2. 'n' is skipped again. The final 'a' brings count to 3. After the loop finishes, count is 3, matching the three a's in "banana". This example leans on two ideas you already have: the in operator testing membership, and the fact that letter, produced by iterating over a string, is itself just a length-1 string that behaves exactly like any other string you have worked with.

Comparing individual characters also works with the ordinary relational operators, since Python compares strings, including length-1 ones, by their underlying code points. 'a' < 'b' is True because ord('a') is less than ord('b'), and this is precisely what lets Python sort words alphabetically and what lets you build simple logic like checking whether a letter falls within a certain range.
